Just now

Two years ago, a friend of mine in Chicago posted on LinkedIn that she’d learned Python in 30 days and landed a data analyst job. Everyone in the comments was hyped. I remember thinking, if she can do it, I can too.
So I made a plan. Thirty days, one hour a day, and by the end I’d be job-ready. That was the goal on paper.
Reality looked very different.
By day five, I was stuck on a “simple” for loop for two hours. By day twelve, I skipped three days in a row because life happened. By day twenty, I almost quit completely.
But I didn’t quit. And what I learned along the way matters more than any 30-day promise you’ll see on YouTube thumbnails. This is the honest version, the one nobody puts in a headline.
The Problem With “Learn Python in 30 Days”
Here’s the thing nobody tells beginners. Thirty days is enough time to learn the basics of Python. It is not enough time to become good at it.
That distinction matters more than people realize.
A student I mentored in Karachi once messaged me in a panic. He said, “I finished a 30-day Python course but I still can’t build anything on my own. Did I fail?”
He didn’t fail. The course did what it promised. It taught him syntax. But syntax and skill are two different things, the same way memorizing grammar rules doesn’t make you a fluent speaker.
Knowing what a for loop does is not the same as knowing when and why to use one in a real project.
Week One: The Motivation High
The first week is always the easiest. You’re excited. You’re watching tutorials, typing along, and everything feels like progress.
I remember feeling unstoppable after day three. I’d learned variables, strings, and basic math operations. I thought, this is easy, why do people say programming is hard?
Then week two happened.
Week Two: Where Most People Quit
This is the week where things stop feeling fun. Loops get confusing. Functions feel abstract. Error messages start showing up that make no sense.
I hit a wall trying to understand functions. I read the same explanation four times and still didn’t get it. I felt genuinely stupid, which is a strange feeling when you’re used to picking things up quickly in other areas of life.
Here’s what nobody tells you. That confused feeling isn’t a sign you’re bad at coding. It’s a sign you’re actually learning something new, and new things feel uncomfortable before they feel natural.
A developer I follow from London once wrote something that stuck with me. She said, “If Python ever starts feeling too easy, you’re probably not challenging yourself enough.” That reframed everything for me. The struggle wasn’t proof I was failing. It was proof I was in the right zone.
The Mistake I Made in Week Three
By week three, I made a classic beginner mistake. I started collecting tutorials instead of writing code.
I’d watch a video about Python projects, feel motivated, bookmark it, and move to the next video without actually building anything. My browser had forty tabs open. My code editor had almost nothing in it.
This is incredibly common, and it happens everywhere, not just to beginners in Pakistan or India who sometimes get blamed for “just watching videos.” I’ve seen the exact same pattern in people from the US and UK too. Watching feels like progress. It isn’t.
The fix was simple but uncomfortable. I closed the tabs and forced myself to build something small and ugly. A basic calculator. Nothing impressive. But it was mine, and I built it by actually typing code, not watching someone else type it.
That one small project taught me more than the previous ten tutorials combined.
A Global Comparison Worth Knowing
One thing that surprised me during this journey was how similar the learning struggle is everywhere, even though access to tools looks different.
In the US or UK, most beginners jump straight into paid platforms like Codecademy or paid Udemy courses, since payment is simple and instant.
In Pakistan and much of South Asia, many beginners start with free YouTube channels or platforms like freeCodeCamp, partly because international payment methods aren’t always accessible, and partly because free resources are genuinely excellent now.
The tools might differ. The confusion in week two doesn’t. Struggling with loops feels the same whether you’re sitting in Boston or Faisalabad.
Week Four: Where It Finally Clicked
By week four, something shifted. I wasn’t fluent, not even close, but I could read code without panicking. I could look at an error message and actually understand what it was telling me instead of just feeling defeated by it.
I built a small project that scraped basic weather data and printed it out. It took me four hours to write about fifteen lines of working code. It wasn’t efficient. It wasn’t clean. But it worked, and I wrote it myself.
That feeling, watching something you built actually run correctly, is different from any tutorial completion certificate. It’s proof, not promise.
What 30 Days Actually Gives You
After finishing my thirty days, here’s my honest assessment. I did not become job-ready. I did not build anything impressive enough to show an employer.
What I did get was the foundation. I understood how to think in small logical steps. I stopped being intimidated by code. I could read documentation without feeling lost.
That foundation is worth more than people give it credit for, because everything after this point becomes about building real projects, not learning new syntax every day.
Three Lessons I’d Give Anyone Starting Today
First, stop collecting tutorials. Pick one resource and stick with it for the full 30 days. Switching between five different courses just resets your progress every time.
Second, build broken things on purpose. Don’t wait until you understand everything perfectly before you start coding. Write messy code, watch it fail, fix it. That process teaches faster than any perfect tutorial ever will.
Third, track small wins, not big goals. I stopped saying “I’m learning Python” and started saying “today I understood how dictionaries work.” Small, specific wins kept me motivated when the big goal felt too far away.
The Truth About Timelines
Thirty days won’t make you an expert. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.
What thirty days can give you is momentum, comfort with the basics, and proof to yourself that you can actually do this. That’s not a small thing. Most people never even get that far, because most people quit around week two, right when things start feeling hard.
If you’re starting your own thirty days right now, whether you’re in New York, Manchester, or Lahore, know this. The struggle in week two isn’t a sign to stop. It’s the exact point where real learning begins.
I almost quit on day twenty. I’m glad I didn’t.
